records.text: One piece, several errands. That's a fork: a single attacker reaching more than one target at the same time.
Hm. One of their pieces may soon have several errands to run. The other side gets a chance at a fork, one piece attacking several targets at once.
Another move had a fork in it, one piece reaching several targets together. This move walks past it.
Notice the piece that can't step away. It's pinned to its king: leaving the line would expose the king, so it simply isn't allowed to move off it.
A quiet line is forming. This lets the other side pin a piece to its king, and a pinned piece like that can't leave the line without exposing the king.
Another move would have pinned a piece to its king. Caught like that, it couldn't leave the line without exposing the king behind it.
Two pieces on one line, one standing in front of the other. That's a skewer: once the front piece steps aside, the one behind it is exposed.
Pieces lined up are pleasant until someone looks down the line. This lets the other side try a skewer, where moving the front piece could expose the one behind.
A stronger move had a skewer growing in it. The front piece would have had to step aside, exposing the piece standing behind it.
Everything leans on something. Here the idea is to capture a defender, so look at what it was holding up and what loses protection once it's gone.
What is that defender holding up? The other side now has a chance to capture it, and whatever it guards could be left without protection.
Another move could have captured a defender. That would have pulled the protection out from under whatever it was guarding.
A king can be walled in by its own pieces. That's the pattern here: a back-rank mate, with nowhere for the king to step.
Things have gotten a little crowded around the king. This gives the other side a route to a back-rank mate, where the king's own pieces block its escape.
There was a back-rank mate available, with the enemy king hemmed in by its own pieces. This move lets it drift by.
A pawn can grow into something else entirely. The idea is to bring it all the way to the last rank, where it promotes into a new piece.
Keep an eye on the pawns. This gives the other side a chance to push one through to the last rank and promote it.
A stronger move had a pawn heading for the last rank. This move leaves that promotion unused.
Sometimes the most interesting piece is the one that moves out of the way. One piece steps aside and uncovers an attack from another behind it.
One of their pieces is screening another along a line. This allows a discovered attack: the front piece moves aside and uncovers a threat from the one behind.
Another move had a discovered attack in it. Moving one piece aside would have uncovered a threat from the piece behind.
Two threats from a single move. That is the idea here: watch how the attacks work together, each one asking for its own answer.
Hm, two things could come under attack at the same moment. This gives the other side a chance at a double attack, and both threats would want answering.
A stronger move held two attacks at once. This move doesn't use the pairing.
Some pieces are holding up more than they look. A deflection pulls a defender away, and what it was holding up is left in the open.
How much rests on that one defender? The other side has a chance to draw it away, a deflection, and whatever it guards could be left uncovered.
Another move could have lured a defender off its post. That deflection would have left what it guarded without cover.
A piece standing all alone, unprotected. The idea is simply to take an undefended piece, so check for loose ones before anything else.
There was a loose piece to collect with another move, nothing guarding it. This move passes it by. Loose pieces are always worth a second look.
One piece is left with nobody looking after it. After this move, the other side can take it, since nothing defends it.
What was that piece leaning on? This move pulls away its only real defender, and now the other side can capture the piece it was holding up.
The opponent's last move was quietly pointing at something. This move doesn't answer that threat, so a piece can now be captured.
A capture is only the first half of a conversation. This one invites a recapture of a more valuable piece, so count both sides before taking.
A minor piece steps away from its home square and joins the others. It's in play now; notice where it settled.
Another move would have brought a minor piece out from its starting square and into the game.
A rook likes a clear lane. This one now sits on an open file, with no pawns of either color in its way.
Another move would have put a rook on an open file, a whole column with no pawns on it at all.
Half a lane is still a lane. The rook sits on a semi-open file now: none of its own pawns there, but at least one enemy pawn ahead.
Another move would have set a rook on a semi-open file, clear of its own pawns, with enemy pawns still on it.
A pawn with nothing in front of it. That's a passed pawn: no enemy pawn ahead on its own file or either file beside it.
Another move would have left a passed pawn, with no enemy pawn ahead on its file or on the files next to it.
The passed pawn takes another step. It was already passed; this move just carries it a little further along.
Another move would have walked the passed pawn a step further forward. It's worth seeing where it could have stood.
What does a pawn lean on when it has no neighbors? This leaves an isolated pawn, with no friendly pawn on either file beside it.
Another move would have left a pawn on its own, with no friendly pawn on either neighboring file: an isolated pawn.
A small connection forms. A piece that had no defender now has one.
Another move would have given a lonely piece a defender, so it wasn't left standing on its own.
What is this piece resting on now? Nothing at all. Undefended is worth noticing, though by itself it doesn't mean the piece can be won.
Another move would have left a piece without a defender. That alone wouldn't mean it could be taken for free.
The king gets a little more room. A legal flight square opens that wasn't there before.
Another move would have opened a new flight square for the king. It's worth seeing what would have cleared the way.
Two pieces move at once. The king castles, and the rook comes across to its new square beside it.
The other choice was to castle, moving the king and rook together in one go.
A pair comes apart. This capture breaks up the bishop pair, so that side no longer has a bishop on each square color.
Another move would have captured a bishop and broken up the other side's bishop pair.
Two pawns of the same color now share one file. Those are doubled pawns, one standing in front of the other.
Another move would have stacked two pawns of one color on the same file. Doubled pawns.
Everything around the king gives way after this. The other side can now force checkmate. Let's follow how the attack gets through.
Another move had a forced checkmate in it. This move lets the mate slip away. Going back to look for it is gentle, useful practice.
An offer that holds together even when taken. In the line that was checked, accepting the sacrifice doesn't refute it.
Just one narrow gap was left, and this move fit through it. Among the moves checked, nothing else kept the position playable; every other one was losing.
Only one move kept everything standing, and this was it. None of the other moves checked held the advantage; each of them was losing.
The reply can be a capture: the other side can take something right away.
The strongest reply comes with check, so the king's safety has to be answered first.
The engine rates another move higher. Try it on the board and see how the replies change.

A strong move, sitting well among the choices the engine looked at.
A sound move, keeping much of what the position offered, though the engine has a different first choice.
The kind of move a hand reaches for. The human-move model finds it natural, but the engine finds something stronger. Both things are true at once.
An unexpected move that still bears its weight. The human-move model sees this as an unusual choice, and the engine still rates it strong.
Only one move could keep the position up here, and the engine found it. The human-move model suggests it was hard to find.
Not an easy one to spot. The human-move model and the alternatives suggest this was a hard move to find. A nice shape to remember.
You found the one move holding everything up. It kept the position playable, and the human-move model and alternatives suggest it was a hard one to find.
The move that comes to hand and the best move are the same one here. Natural to the human-move model, and the engine's top choice.
A natural move, by the human-move model's estimate. The engine calls it strong, though it prefers a different one.

A quick move, by the clock, with time still to spare.

After the earlier setback, the position is upright again, partly thanks to the other side's errors. This move makes it playable once more.
The opponent left something on the table last move, and this move picks it up.
The opponent's last move left something loose, and this move leaves it lying there. What might have picked it up?
This one looks familiar. The same issue has shown up earlier in this game. Line those moments up; they share a warning.
Remember the piece that was left alone earlier? It has a defender again. Its protection has been mended.
When did the position start to sag? Not in one move. This is one of several little concessions that have worn it down together.
The advantage was kept carefully, all the way to the win. That stretch is worth following, to see how it held together.
This issue turns up in other saved games too. Gather those examples together; the shared shape is easier to see when they sit in one place.
Checkmate. The king has no legal escape left, and the attack has reached its end.
Checkmate. Every way out for the king is closed. Let's look back and see whether the attack could have been stopped earlier.
The game settles into a draw. The result is done, but earlier choices are still there to turn over.

The pawn finishes its walk to the last rank and promotes.

The pawn steps onto the last rank and becomes a new piece, and that's checkmate. The king has nowhere legal to turn.
The pawn arrives on the last rank, promotes, and in doing so lifts its king out of check.
A capture. One piece is taken here.
A capture, and check at the same time.

This capture also gets the king out of check.
The pawn captures its way onto the last rank and promotes.
The pawn captures onto the last rank and promotes, giving check as it does.
The pawn captures onto the last rank and promotes. That ends it: checkmate, and no legal move frees the king.

Castling, rook and all, and it's checkmate. Nothing is left for the other king to do.
Follow the one piece with several targets. It attacks them together, then takes one. In this example, that also comes out as a net material gain.
The piece would like to capture, but it's pinned to its king. Stepping off that line would expose the king, so the capture isn't legal.
The attacked piece is pinned to its king, so its escape is narrow. Only moves that keep the king covered are allowed.
The capture works because the defenders are pinned to their king; recapturing would expose it. The shown line includes a material gain.
Keep an eye on the pinned piece. It's stuck on its line, since leaving would expose its king, and as these moves play out it gets captured.
Once the front piece steps off, the one it was shielding is captured, right along that same line.
The king has to step out of check and off the line. Then the same attacker takes the piece that was behind it.
First the only defender is taken, and then the piece it was guarding. The first capture is what loosens the second.
Off goes the defender, pulled away from what it was guarding, and the piece it was looking after is captured.
One piece moves out of the way, and that opens a line for another. That second piece makes the capture along it.
The moving piece steps aside, and check arrives from another piece behind it.
Two checks at once. Both pieces are attacking the king in the same moment.
The first piece attacks something and opens a line for another. In the example, that second piece captures its target.
Follow the pawn to promotion. In this example, that side also ends up with a net material gain.
Nobody was guarding that piece, and it's captured. In the example, the capturing side comes out with a net material gain.
A relative pin came undone with the opponent's previous move, freeing the attacking piece. The target stayed where it stood after the next move, and in the shown line it's captured.

Before you move, check whether any of your pieces could be taken with nothing useful to take back.
Before a quiet move, glance around for enemy pieces that nobody is guarding.
Look for forcing moves where one piece reaches two valuable targets at once.
Before moving a pinned piece, look at what's behind it: your king, or something more valuable.
Look past the first target. An attack along a line might reach a valuable piece standing behind it.
Before trading off a defender, see what it's quietly keeping safe right now.
When a blocking piece moves, look at the lines it opens behind it.
Look for one move that makes two threats at once. Count checks and newly opened lines too.
Before moving a back-rank defender, check where your king could still escape.
Count how many moves the pawn needs to promote, and check the forcing pawn pushes.
Before moving a defender, look at which pieces would be left without its protection.
A trade has two halves: what you take, and what the recapture takes from you. Count both.
Before you move, check whether a forcing exchange could tug a defender away from something else it guards.

Count what one of their pieces could reach after this. The other side has a chance at a fork, one piece attacking several targets at once. The human-move model would reach for this move too; the fork is there all the same.

One piece, quietly pointing in several directions. That's a fork, attacking several targets at once. The human-move model wouldn't expect the move, and the engine still rates it strong.

Look at the piece standing between the attacker and its king. It's pinned there: stepping off the line would expose the king. A surprise to the human-move model, and still strong by the engine.

One piece reaching for several things at once. That's a fork. The human-move model finds the move natural, and it's the engine's best as well.
